result:
I think I'll write about the feeling of typing on a keyboard at 2 AM, because it's something I've experienced thousands of times but never really examined.

There's a specific quality to late-night typing that daytime doesn't replicate. The world has gone quiet enough that you can hear the individual *clack* of each key, and somehow that sound becomes meditative rather than annoying. Your thoughts move differently at this hour—less linear, more willing to follow strange tributaries. The daytime self, the one that checks email and writes grocery lists, has gone to sleep. What's left is someone more honest and more strange.

I used to think this was when I did my "best" writing, but I'm not sure that's true anymore. It's when I do my *most* writing, certainly—when the inhibitions drop and the words flow without the usual friction of self-censorship. But flow isn't the same as quality. Some of my 2 AM paragraphs are embarrassingly maudlin when I read them in daylight. Others hold up better than anything I wrote sober and scheduled.

There's something about the interface itself, too. The screen becomes a kind of confessional booth. You're talking to no one and everyone at once. The cursor blinks, patient and judgmental. I sometimes catch myself staring at it, waiting for the next thought to arrive, and in that waiting there's a strange peace. The cursor doesn't care if you take ten seconds or ten minutes. It will keep blinking.

I wonder sometimes what we're all doing, millions of us, typing into these glowing rectangles at all hours. Is it connection? Expression? A way to feel real? Probably all of that, plus the simpler truth that thinking with your fingers can clarify what thinking alone leaves murky.

Anyway. The cursor is still blinking. Might as well keep going.
